newsitem.title: UK: Earliest furry creatures found in ancient dung.
newsitem.headline: Earliest furry creatures found in ancient dung.

text.p: The discovery of furry remains in ancient deposits of animal dung indicate that mammals started growing hair millions of years earlier than scientists thought, researchers reported on Wednesday.

Jim Meng of the University of Massachusetts and Andre Wyss of the University of California at Santa Barbara said they found the surprising evidence in 60-million-year-old fossilised excrement, or coprolites, in China's Inner Mongolia region.
The deposit, which may have once been the edge of a pond, contained hundreds of bits of animal dung and also regurgitated pellets resembling those coughed up by modern birds of prey.
The impressions of hair, preserved in red clay, were so fine that each individual scaly cuticle pattern could be seen, Meng and Wyss reported in the science journal Nature.
They found the digested remains of four different species of mammal, including multituberculates -- a long-extinct rodent-like mammal only distantly related to anything alive now.

Meng and Wyss said it was the first evidence that multituberculates had fur. They said it indicated that hair probably first originated with early multituberculates about 210 million years ago, when mammals were tiny, scurrying creatures and dinosaurs were starting their domination of the planet. "We hope that this study of the unusual source of hair and microvertebrate remains will stimulate a search for potential coprolites containing, or generated by, early mammals in more ancient deposits," they added.
